newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall again, bonds end lower.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall again, bonds end lower.

text.p: Stocks fell again Thursday as the Dow Jones industrial average ended below 6,000 for the first time in two weeks amid stepped-up profit-taking.
Bonds also lost ground and the dollar ended mixed.

The 30-share Dow dropped 43.98 points to 5,992.48 after sliding 58 points over the first three days of the week. It was the first close below 6,000 since Oct. 10 for the world's most widely watched stock index.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,203 to 1,112 on heavy volume of 415 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"We started a correction on Monday and we're still in it," said Alfred Goldman, technical research director of A.G. Edwards. "It's a backing-and-filling affair that might wear people out for a week or two."
He said the profit-taking was in the shares of oil, household products and food companies that had been strong recently.
The Dow rode a wild rollercoaster in the afternoon, losing nearly 50 points before bouncing back and then retreating at the close.
The shares of big oil companies fell as crude oil prices sank after soaring to a post-Gulf War high of more than $26 a barrel on supply worries.
"People are itchy to take profits," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/Twenty-First. "It's easy to rationalise. It's a choppy, marking time day."
The Treasury bond market fell on news that weekly jobless claims fell more than expected to 320,000 for the week ended Oct. 19, indicating that the nation's labour market remains tight.
The benchmark 30-year bond lost a quarter point, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.85 percent from 6.83 percent on Wednesday.
Wall Street is awaiting Friday's release of September durable goods orders. Economists are predicting a 2.0 percent increase.
In currency markets, the dollar fell against the German mark after the Bundesbank held interest rates steady. The dollar also fell against the Japanese yen but rose against other major currencies.

The council of the German central bank, or Bundesbank, voted at a meeting Thursday to hold rates steady, confirming public comments a day earlier by Bundesbank officials saying they saw no reason to expect lower rates ahead.
Lower rates in Germany would spur the sluggish German economy but would also tend to weaken the mark in the short run by reducing returns on mark-based assets.
"The Deutschemark should continue to strengthen, since now they don't expect a rate cut in Germany," said Dori Schwartz, associate international economist at Donaldson Lufkin and Jenrette.
The dollar fell to 1.5175 marks late in New York from 1.5215 late on Wednesday. It also slipped to 112.82 Japanese yen from 112.95.
The British pound edged lower to $1.5955 from $1.5967. The dollar rose to 1.2557 Swiss francs from 1.2540 and climbed to Canadian $1.3453 from C$1.3438.
Elsewhere, crude oil for December delivery fell 35 cents to $24.51 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE index fell 29 points to 3,999.4 and Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average lost 78.66 points to end at 21,003.49.
